content: This document is an updated review of the use of steroids for treating idiopathic sudden sensorineural hearing loss (ISSHL), a condition characterized by sudden hearing loss of cochlear or retrocochlear origin without an identifiable cause. Steroids are frequently prescribed for this condition, but their effectiveness remains a topic of debate. The primary objective of the review was to assess whether steroids improve hearing in patients with ISSHL. A secondary objective was to evaluate whether steroids reduce tinnitus. Additionally, the review aimed to determine the incidence of significant side effects associated with steroid use. The authors conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Ear, Nose and Throat Disorders Group Trials Register, CENTRAL, PubMed, EMBASE, and others, for both published and unpublished trials. The most recent search was performed on April 22, 2013. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs), with or without blinding, that compared steroids to either no treatment or placebo. Trials involving steroids in combination with other treatments were included only if the control group received the same additional treatment. Two authors independently reviewed the full-text articles of potentially relevant trials and applied the inclusion criteria. The trials were assessed for risk of bias using the Cochrane methodology. Data extraction was standardized and cross-checked by the authors. Investigators were contacted when additional information was required. Due to the heterogeneity of the study populations, as well as differences in steroid formulations, dosages, and treatment durations, meta-analysis was deemed inappropriate. Instead, the results of each study were analyzed and reported individually, and a narrative overview of the findings was provided. Three trials, involving a total of 267 participants, met the inclusion criteria. However, all three studies were determined to have a high risk of bias. The findings of these trials were inconsistent: 1. One trial found no significant improvement in hearing among patients treated with oral steroids compared to the placebo group. 2. A second trial reported a significant improvement in hearing in 61% of patients receiving oral steroids, compared to 32% in the control group (which included both placebo-treated and untreated participants). 3. The third trial also found no significant improvement in hearing with oral steroids compared to placebo. However, this study had notable methodological issues, including non-adherence to strict inclusion criteria, significant exclusion of participants from the final analysis, and poor compliance with the treatment protocol. Regarding side effects, two trials did not provide clear evidence of any harmful effects associated with steroid use. One study explicitly stated that no adverse effects were observed in patients receiving steroid treatment. The authors concluded that the effectiveness of steroids in treating ISSHL remains uncertain. The evidence from the included RCTs is contradictory, and the small sample sizes of the studies limit the reliability of the findings. Further high-quality research is needed to clarify the role of steroids in managing this condition.
